Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Tuesday, 11 June 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 032)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR MUSTON: Thank you, Commissioner. We are commencing
this short hearing block, which over the next four days
will examine three fairly discrete issues. The first is
the Sydney Children's network, which will be examined today
and Friday. St Vincent's Hospital we will be looking at on
Wednesday, and the Hawkesbury District Health Service,
which has been operated most recently by St John of God
under a PPP, will be looked at on Thursday. In respect of
the latter, we note that it is shortly to be handed back to
the state.
In terms of the children's network, we're not going to
look, during this hearing block, at what have been
described in some of the submissions and statements
provided as the "inadequacy or unsuitability of ABF
funding" for the recognition and funding of complex
paediatric services. That's not because we're not going to
look at them, but it's because we think it's probably more
appropriate to defer them to the funding hearing block a
little bit later in the year.
We are going to examine how the network operates and
whether, as some have suggested, it's really a network in
name only. And it is important for us to develop an
understanding of the potential benefits of a properly
networked system of paediatric care across the state and,
to the extent that we don't currently enjoy that, what
might be done to better facilitate it.
In this respect, we anticipate that we'll probably see
some similar themes emerging to those which rattled out of
the evidence given in relation to the spinal care or spinal
injury services and the catastrophic brain injury services
a little bit earlier in the Commission, where the benefits
of a properly networked system were identified and some of
the challenges presented by the absence of a good and
functioning network similarly were identified.
Turning then to St Vincent's and Hawkesbury District
Health Service, these are probably, we anticipate, likely
to raise some similar issues to those which emerged from
evidence given by Royal Rehab, Tresillian and Karitane.
There are some subtle but important differences, though.
St Vincent's is a networked AHO, I think the only networked
AHO, which means it has its service agreement directly with

the ministry, as opposed to those other entities which have
their service agreements entered into with LHDs. We'll
examine the benefits and disbenefits of that.
We're also then going to look at the arrangements
under which St John of God has operated the Hawkesbury
service. As I mentioned a moment ago, that has been in the
nature of a PPP. The contractual arrangements that St John
of God have had in respect of the arrangements of that
service have been with the Nepean Blue Mountains LHD, not
the ministry, so it's a subtle difference between them and
St Vincent's. More importantly, we're going to explore
with the witnesses called in respect of that facility the
reasons that they have chosen to bring that arrangement to
an end.
Ultimately, though, we anticipate that both
St Vincent's and St John of God will raise issues about the
extent to which the funding provided under their respective
arrangements is sufficient to meet the costs of the
delivery of the services that they are required to deliver
under those agreements. As each are private entities and
not LHDs or part of the state, the drivers for them and the
consequences of funding deficits are obviously very
different.
Finally we anticipate exploring with both St Vincent's
and St John of God the extent to which they are involved or
they have been involved in the planning of health services
in the wider catchments that they operate, that is to say,
whether there is any particular long-term strategy or
planning around the particular services that each of those
facilities offered relative to facilities within that wider
catchment.
We've discussed and heard evidence throughout the
Commission about the way in which the delivery of health
care is a patchwork of services which pulls together to, as
best as possible, cover all of the needs of the community.
It has been identified for us that there is a real
importance to ensure that there is no overlap and,
similarly, that there are no important gaps. We are
interested to explore with St Vincent's and St John of God
the extent to which they are involved, if at all, in that
process of identifying what the landscape looks like and
exactly where they fit in it with a view to minimising any
gaps and avoiding any overlap.

Without further ado, we'll turn to the children's
network. Mr Glover is going take those witnesses.
THE COMMISSIONER: Just before we do, just so everyone is
aware of what I've been looking at, other than obviously
the witness outlines, two of the things I've read are the
"Final report of the expert panel" regarding "Review of
governance for the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network" -
I think the shorthand for it is "the Alexander review" -
and the "Review of health services for children, young
people and families within the NSW Health system", the
shorthand for which is "the Henry review". The Alexander
review is June 2019. The Henry review is December of that
year.
One of the things Professor Henry says he was asked to
do - sorry, I will go back a step. I would like to know
with clarity what, if any, of the Alexander review
recommendations were accepted. I would like to know -
I think I already do - about Professor Henry. Someone has
told me that all of the 77, I think, recommendations were
accepted and some have been implemented.
The things I don't understand are why Professor Henry
was asked to address a review that was six months before
his own. I could be misreading it, but there are aspects
of Professor Henry's review where he comments on what the
Alexander review found, that I think are - they don't seem
to be correct. They seem to be misinterpretations of the
Alexander review, which concerns me if the Henry review
recommendations have all been accepted.
There are also some references to these reviews in the
witness statements that I don't completely follow. I won't
take that up now, but I would like it explored in the
evidence.
MR MUSTON: These are matters that will be explored in the
evidence, and otherwise it may be for my learned friends to
enlighten your Honour in respect of some of the motivation
questions that --
THE COMMISSIONER: I thought I would say that now so that
people are aware of what I've been looking at and what's
confusing me.

MR MUSTON: Thank you, Commissioner.
MR GLOVER: The first witness is Dr Alexander.
THE COMMISSIONER: For clarity, a different Alexander than
the "Alexander review"; correct?
MR GLOVER: Yes. I laboured under that misapprehension
for a short while.
<SHIRLEY MARIE ALEXANDER, sworn: [10.08am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR GLOVER:
MR GLOVER: Q. Dr Alexander, could you state your full
name, please?
A. Shirley Marie Alexander.
Q. You are a staff specialist at the Sydney Children's
Hospitals Network; correct?
A. I am.
Q. You have been in that role since July 2008; is that
right?
A. Yes. I've actually worked there since 2007 but as
staff specialist since 2008.
Q. You are currently the head of department of the
Children's Hospital Institute of Sports Medicine and Weight
Management; correct?
A. Correct.
Q. And you have held that role since about October 2016;
is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. For the purposes of giving your evidence today, you
made a statement on 6 June; is that right?
A. Yes, I think so.
Q. It is on the last page.
A. Yes, yes, that's right.
Q. I will bring it up on the screen for you. It is
[MOH.9999.1286.0001]. It's just up on the screen there to
your right, although if you have a hard copy, feel free to
use that. Have you had a chance to read the statement

again before giving your evidence today?
A. I have, yes.
Q. I understand there is one correction that you wish to
make to paragraph 11; is that right?
A. There is.
Q. In the last sentence?
A. Yes, it should be, "If referrals are not accepted,
services should find appropriate or instigate appropriate
alternative treatment routes" --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. I'm sorry, I've just missed that.
What line are we at?
A. The very last line in paragraph 11.
Q. So it should say?
A. "If referrals are not accepted", apologies for that,
"services should find appropriate alternative treatment
routes/suggestions for the referrer to action."
THE COMMISSIONER: The statement I've got, that was put in
my folder, differs from this. Is that a problem?
MR GLOVER: Well, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: I will change that. That is a problem.
MR GLOVER: That is a problem. I need to correct that,
Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: There have obviously been some changes
made to the statements since they were provided to me.
MR GLOVER: I'm sorry.
THE COMMISSIONER: Does that apply to many or all of the
statements?
MR GLOVER: It does, some. I now can't immediately recall
whether the other two for today, but, Commissioner, you
should have the right version.
THE COMMISSIONER: I was given a hard copy, which I have
worked on. It is possible that a different version was
emailed to me, but I've assumed that there have been no
changes and kept the hard copies because that's what I've

highlighted and got notes on.
MR GLOVER: Yes, all entirely sensible.
THE COMMISSIONER: I can probably live with what's on the
screen at the moment.
MR GLOVER: All right. I think if you are happy to
proceed in that way, we can manage it for this witness.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes. Perhaps I should just ask,
ballpark, really - lots of fundamental changes to the
statements or only minor?
MR GLOVER: To about three or four paragraphs and nothing
that altered the substance of the evidence, is my
recollection.
THE COMMISSIONER: Let's live with what's on the screen
and what I've got, but I would like a copy of the actual
witness's statement at some stage.
MR GLOVER: I'm sure that would be very helpful.
Q. All right, Dr Alexander, none of that is your fault --
THE COMMISSIONER: Obviously, moving forward, when there
are changes to witness statements and I've been given
a hard copy, people will let me know and give me the new
updated version?
MR GLOVER: I'm sure they will.
Q. Now, Dr Alexander, in paragraph 6 of your statement,
there you tell us that one of the benefits of the network
structure is that it supports greater coordination and
collaboration across clinical services in both hospitals;
do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. When you were referring to the "network structure" in
that paragraph, you're talking about the two facilities
that sit within the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network;
correct?
A. Yes.
Q. In paragraph 7, you tell us that since the development

of the network, more services have collaborated and shared
knowledge processes to support each other. So by that, do
we understand that since the development or the
implementation of the network in about 2010, more and more
services, over time, have collaborated and coordinated
their services; is that a fair summary of those two
paragraphs?
A. Yes, that's my perception, yes.
Q. Are you aware of services that haven't done that -
that is, haven't collaborated and integrated their
services?
A. Not specifically.
Q. Are you aware of any barriers to that collaboration
and coordination of services within the network?
A. Not specifically. I mean, barriers would potentially
be more maybe on a departmental and individual level.
Q. What do you mean by that?
A. In terms of where interests of head of departments or
staff lie as to, you know, where their special interests
are.
Q. When you say "the interests of head of departments and
their special interests", does that mean that there may be
a disconnect between the interests of a department at one
facility versus the interests of a department at another
facility? Is that what you are describing?
A. There could be.
Q. Could be? When you say --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Could we just go back a step.
Sorry - no, you finish that question, because I am
interrupting you mid-flow. I will wait.
MR GLOVER: Q. When you said "could be" to my last
question, is that something that you actually have any
knowledge of, or is it just a potential?
A. It's just a potential, not that I have specific
knowledge.
THE COMMISSIONER: Is that a convenient time?
Q. Can we just go back a step and perhaps look at
paragraphs 2 and 3 of your statement. In paragraph 2 you

have introduced what we call the Sydney Children's
Hospitals Network, and from then on, you are referring to
the network and, as an example, in the last sentence of 3
you are saying, "Having a Network has enabled ...",
et cetera. Do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. "Sydney Children's Hospitals Network" is just a title.
When you make a reference to the "network", how would you
define it? What does it involve?
A. To me, the network is looking at - it's two separate
hospitals but one entity, with the aim of providing
optimised care for the children from a tertiary and
quaternary perspective of New South Wales, and also for
their local population, from the secondary care level,
and --
Q. Is it networked at that secondary level?
A. Is it networked at the secondary level? Sorry.
Q. Well, when you are talking about local populations, is
that part of the network? Do you mean serving the local
populations, that Randwick services the east and
south-eastern suburbs and Westmead the western suburbs,
I suppose; is that what you mean by that?
A. Yes.
Q. Is that part of the network, though?
A. It is to a degree part of the network, but secondary
level care is --
Q. To what degree is it part of the network?
A. In the sense that you're still looking at the best -
the optimised care for your local population as well as the
New South Wales population, and, you know, if, for
example --
Q. How is the Randwick Hospital networked to the Westmead
Hospital for the purposes of doing that - taking the word
"networked" to mean joined in some way, collaborating in
some way?
A. Yes. So, for example, some of the ambulatory care
services, even though they are - they're working at both
levels, at a tertiary and a secondary level, and if you're
looking at secondary level, if that service, which is
a networked service, such as hospital in the home - if, for
example - but they have staff at both sites - if they are

understaffed at one site and maybe have more patients that
they have to go and visit, for example, and the other site
has less visits booked in for that day and more staff
available, they share services, and that could be at the
sort of secondary level, patient level, but also they can
do that for the tertiary. So there is a melding, you know.
Because the hospitals both are - they are secondary and
tertiary/quaternary, that can sort of be a grey area. So
it's - you're networked on all levels, I think.
Q. Sorry, what do you mean by "grey area"?
A. Well, if you're at other, for example, some
metropolitan hospitals, rural/regional hospitals, they are
secondary level care and they won't provide tertiary level
care, whereas because both sites, Sydney Children's
Hospital and Children's Hospital Westmead, provide both
secondary and tertiary level, there can be a little bit of
a blurring of the --
Q. I see. All right. Does that cover - I'm obviously
not asking you to go down to the detail, but in terms of
the big picture, that's what you mean by "network" or what
your understanding is, it has a network?
A. Yes, well, overall the network is to work both
collaboratively - both sites collaboratively and
coordinatedly, but also networking within the LHDs within
New South Wales from that sort of tertiary level.
Q. And how does that work?
A. So, for example, there have been new services set up,
like virtualKIDS, which was - it's a remote monitoring
service. That was commenced during COVID, and that has now
become - it's expanded and it's now become a service that
actually services the whole of New South Wales. During
COVID, it was mainly for the two sites, and then we got
asked to, you know, support some of the other
rural/regional areas that were having challenges, and then
it's now become a network - a New South Wales statewide
service.
Q. Just because we're on paragraph 3, can I ask you some
questions that are just out of curiosity but completely
different to what we were just exploring?
A. Yes, sure.
Q. In paragraph 3 you talk about the increase in the
prevalence of, first of all, obesity. Obviously, these are

obesity rates in children or people under 18?
A. Yes.
Q. Off the top of your head, are you able to help me with
what the increase is and what the levels are?
A. Well, one in four children, school-aged children, in
New South Wales have issues with overweight or obesity.
The overweight prevalence has levelled off, but obesity has
increased from about 6 per cent to 8 per cent.
Q. I just missed what - my computer's down, I can't see
the running transcript. You said "all weights", did you?
A. Overweight. Overweight.
Q. Tell me the difference, the medical difference,
between overweight and obesity?
A. Overweight is related to the body mass index of
a child, which will be between the 85th and the 95th
percentile on age and gender/sex-specific growth charts,
BMI charts; and obesity is above the 95th percentile, and
obesity basically is when excess adipose tissue in the body
starts to create health problems.
Q. And when you are talking about increase in prevalence
of obesity, can you give me an idea about what that
increase has been over a time period, or --
A. So over about the last 10 years, it's increased from
about 6 per cent to 8 per cent, but the severity of the
obesity - so those at the severe end of obesity have
increased even more. So, for example, when I first started
working in the area, we rarely got children that were over
100 kilograms. Now we have children up to 250, 280, 300.
So that severity has increased.
Q. Is the concern for that not just immediate health
problems but health problems into adulthood, I imagine?
A. Yes. I mean, there are health and psychosocial
problems involved in that.
Q. The extension of service you mention in paragraph 3
with the dietician weight management clinics, what does
that involve? What are they exactly?
A. We now have a position which we call a network
dietician position, so the dietician works two days at one
site, two days at another site, and prior to that - so
that's been about 12 months. Prior to that, there was no
specific weight management service at Randwick. Now --

Q. Sorry, has this been set up because of the increase in
prevalence that you have been talking about, the concern
that --
A. Yes, we've been working on it for a little while --
Q. Yes, yes. Sorry, I interrupted you. Keep going.
A. No, that's all right. And so even though the
prevalence of obesity is less in the eastern suburbs,
because obesity tends to be a higher prevalence in lower
socioeconomic areas, there is still a need for weight
management services in that area. And also the Aboriginal
population has a very high prevalence. So we felt that
we've been sort of working towards having a network service
to provide intervention for children affected by obesity at
both sites.
Q. And the last question on that, obviously - well,
perhaps not obviously, but my assumption is that the
purpose of the weight management clinics is to have
improved health and lower weight. How is that done through
the clinics? What is actually done?
A. So the dietician will give dietary advice on how to -
it's really looking at lifestyle goals around nutrition and
also some physical activity. If the young person involved
has more health concerns or more severe obesity - so the
dietician-only clinics look at children with less severe
obesity, then the dietician liaises with the team overall,
because we all meet on a regular basis, and would be
referred to our multidisciplinary team that's based at the
Children's Hospital at Westmead. The ultimate goal would
be to have both services across both sites, as in dietician
and also a multidisciplinary team, but the dietician at the
Randwick site has access to the full expertise of the team.
Q. The ultimate goal you just referred to obviously
requires that ultimate goal to be funded?
A. It would require resourcing and --
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, okay. Sorry for that diversion.
Go ahead.
MR GLOVER: Q. Dr Alexander, if I could take you back to
your statement and turn to paragraph 9. There you tell us
that, "One of the limitations of the network structure is
the cultural impact caused by the creation of the network
itself." Do you see that?

A. Yes.
Q. I think from your earlier answers, you were employed
in the service, which is now the network, both before and
after its creation?
A. (Witness nods).
Q. So you have seen the transition firsthand, I take it?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. What do you mean in the first sentence there about,
"One of the limitations of the network structure is the
cultural impact caused by the creation of the network
itself"?
A. So my observation, having not worked at - so I was
originally employed at the Children's Hospital at Westmead,
but it was only a couple of years before the network was
put in place. However, you know, I've worked in a number
of hospitals across both Australia and the UK, and my
understanding is that people that have worked at both sides
for a long time, for example - and over the years and
decades, each site has developed its own culture, its own
sort of personality, its own way of working, and they can
be quite different in some areas, and I think whenever you
have a change and a merging of entities together, there
will be some that will be early adopters of change and
there will be some that are more resistant to the change.
And there is also a feeling of, even though we are
a network, we still want to maintain that sort of
individuality of the culture at each different site. Just
because we can coordinate and collaborate together doesn't
mean to say that you need to lose that sort of cultural
identity.
Q. I will break that up a little bit. Some of the issues
you have described in that last answer create a barrier of
sorts to the integration and collaboration of services that
you described earlier in your evidence; is that right?
A. Yes.
Q. Is that something that persists today, or has it all
been overcome, to your observation?
A. I think some of it persists today and it's a work in
progress. I think overall what we are - I mean, ultimately
what we all aim for is to do the right thing by the right
patient at the right time at the right place, you know,
optimise health care, and people, some people, might want

to do it in slightly different ways. I think whenever you
have a collaboration together, you've got to take into
account other people's ideas or ideals. For some that
might be easier, and for others it might take a bit longer,
and so I think it's still a work in progress.
Q. We're now almost 15 years down the track. What
initiatives, to the extent you are aware of them, have been
put in place to finally close that loop?
A. Well, I think during COVID there was a lot of
collaboration. We worked together very well, made changes
very quickly, as they were needed during COVID. I think,
based on that, there has been a lot of good work, a lot of
trust built up and a lot of collaborative projects and
services built up, like virtualKIDS, that have come from
that. So I - sorry, I have lost train of your - just ask
me your question again.
Q. I will ask a different question. To the extent that
these issues still persist today, what do you think could
be done to overcome them?
A. I think for most people, when you are looking at
change and doing something that might be different from the
way that they've done things before, it's to do with
communication, being heard, feeling like you are part of
the process of change and that you can give input to the
process and then seeing that what you have suggested or
your ideas and your input is being acted upon.
Q. Can I take you to paragraph 10, please. This touches
on some of the answers that you gave to the Commissioner
earlier. I just want to make sure I have understood what
you say in paragraph 10, and then I will ask you some
further questions about it. In paragraph 10, you tell us
that the network operates to provide support for regional
and rural communities through virtualKIDS and outreach
clinics but is not always best placed or resourced to
deliver paediatric services across the state. By that, do
we understand it that the network provides support to
paediatric departments in LHDs across the state, who will
then have primary carriage of the care for children in
those services; correct?
A. Yes.
Q. But the network itself will not be the primary care
deliverer. Is that what you mean?
A. Yes.

Q. How does that operate on a day-to-day basis, that sort
of approach?
A. So overall, and again particularly since COVID,
there's been the - telehealth has accelerated, and so
that's enabled many services to do, if you like, virtual
outreach clinics and support, so the local clinician can
connect with someone in the network for their expertise and
support, and they can do that either with their patient
connecting with the expert and then the expert or the
network person connecting with the local clinician, or they
can do it with the local clinician being in the room, so
there's many ways that the network clinicians can support
local services at regional/rural areas, by joint care,
joint coordinated care.
Q. Is this something that your department does?
A. We do more and more of that now, yes, because regional
and rural areas don't have weight management services.
Q. Perhaps let's use your department as an example.
A. Yes.
Q. Take me through how the process would work. So there
is a paediatrician in Wagga, who has a presentation of
someone who needs the services of your expertise.
A. Yes.
Q. How would they go about getting the support from the
network that you described in paragraph 10?
A. So they would refer to our service and then we would
liaise with them as to whether or not the patient meets the
referral criteria, for example. Then we would also -
depending on how far they are away, our clinical nurse
consultant would discuss with the family as to whether or
not they would want to actually come up for a physical
examination and interview or consultation in our service.
If not, then what we would do would be, we would liaise
with the local clinician to do the physical examination,
but we would link up with the family to do a consult via
telehealth. Often that's the family on their own.
Sometimes it's with the clinician in the room with them.
And then we devise a plan of how often to connect with the
family or the clinician.
Often what we encourage is local facilities, so, for
example, we might get the local dietician to connect with

the family and the local paediatrician, and then our
dietician would also liaise with that local dietician to
give support and advice as to how to move forward with the
family, and then the local dietician, local paediatrician,
would see the patient more frequently and then we would see
them on a monthly or a three-monthly basis to connect up
and give further support. And then obviously we're
available for queries from the local services. They might
email us, might phone us, as to further advice as to what
to do or interpret results, et cetera. So that's the way
it would work, and I suspect many other services do that.
Q. Are there any formal plans or pathways that identify
how support from a regional clinician through to a service
like yours can be obtained?
A. So we have different pathways, our service has
different pathways. We are in the process of formalising
a model of care for regional/rural support. It's not
finalised as yet, but, yes, that would be the way we would
do it, would be sort of a clinical pathway that the
clinicians could follow.
Q. In providing support of the kind that you have just
described, would there be benefit, in your view, to there
being a high-level overarching plan for the delivery of
paediatric care across the state?
A. I think a higher overarching plan across the state
would definitely be helpful in terms of developing services
as evidence-based and need. There would have to be I think
the facility to look at specific areas, so that different
areas would - you know, they will have different needs,
different requirements, different, you know, population
prevalence with that condition, so you would need to build
in to that overarching plan or policy, or whatever, to be
able to be flexible with the different areas and the
different sub-specialties.
Q. Is what you are suggesting that there needs to be an
assessment of the needs for paediatric care in different
parts of the state as part of that planning process?
A. Usually that's what you would do. You would do
a needs analysis to see what specifically is needed in what
area.
Q. And as part of that plan development, would there be
benefit in identifying clearly the types of services that,
for example, the network would provide and the types of

services that ought to be available in the LHDs across the
state in relation to paediatric care?
A. Yes, I think so.
Q. And would there be benefit in clearly identifying the
support that the network could give to paediatric units in
the LHDs across the state and the mechanisms by which that
support could be obtained?
A. Yes, I think so.
Q. Does any of that exist at the moment, to your
knowledge?
A. Yes, I think in virtualKIDS, for example, with that
going statewide, they have - you know, there is a definite
remit, there are definite pathways for clinicians and
families to follow, and it's also expanding into different
areas. You know, they've got the - they're looking at new
models of care as to how virtualKIDS can support patients
and families and clinicians to avoid admission to or
presentation to emergency or enable discharge home more
safely and more early.
Q. So that's an example of a particular service having
a pathway and a plan; correct?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. Is there anything, though, to your knowledge, that
